title: German Alphabet, Pronunciation, Numbers, and Time
description: Why German matters, how many people speak it, career and study opportunities — then dive into the alphabet, pronunciation, numbers, and telling time.
content: German is the most widely spoken native language in the EU, with ~130 million native speakers and a massive impact on science, engineering, and business. This unit starts with why you should learn German: job opportunities, tuition-free universities, scientific publishing, and cultural access. Then it moves into the German alphabet (26 letters + 4 special characters), pronunciation rules, numbers 1-99999, telling time in both formal (24h) and informal (12h) formats, and finishes with hundreds of English-German cognates to quickly build your vocabulary.

title: German Sounds: Diphthongs, Consonants, and Pronunciation
description: Master all German sounds: vowel pairs (diphthongs), consonant combinations, the German R, the glottal stop, and a complete reference table for every letter sound.
content: German has a small, fixed set of diphthongs and consonant combinations that are pronounced the exact same way every single time. Unlike English, there are no surprises. This unit covers every sound pattern you need to read any German word correctly, including vowel lengths, consonant clusters, the German R, and the glottal stop.

The German R — start, middle, and end of words
The glottal stop — separating vowel-starting words
Complete vowel sound reference table (short vs long)

title: German Nouns, Gender, and Articles
description: A complete introduction to German nouns and their articles: three genders, 200 high-frequency nouns organized by category, definite/indefinite/negative articles, capitalization rules, compound nouns, and memory techniques.
content: Every German noun has a grammatical gender: masculine (der), feminine (die), or neuter (das). Gender determines which article to use. This unit covers 200 essential real-world nouns organized by gender and category, plus definite (der/die/das), indefinite (ein/eine), and negative (kein/keine) articles, rules for capitalization and compound nouns, and effective memorization strategies.

The golden rule: learn nouns with their articles

title: Pronouns in German
description: For dummies: German personal, possessive, and demonstrative pronouns explained simply with pronunciation, examples, practice exercises, and cultural tips.
content: Pronouns replace nouns so you don't repeat yourself. In German, you must match pronouns to the noun's gender (der = masculine, die = feminine, das = neuter). Unlike English where everything is 'it', German uses 'er' for der-words, 'sie' for die-words, and 'es' for das-words. This unit also covers the three ways to say 'you' (du for one friend, ihr for a group, Sie for strangers/bosses), possessive pronouns (mein, dein, sein, ihr, unser, euer) that change endings like 'ein/eine', and demonstratives (dieser, diese, dieses) pointing to specific things. Includes cheat sheets, flowcharts, dialogues, and practice exercises with answers.
subtopics: What is a pronoun? Why German is different from English
9 personal pronouns with pronunciation tips and memory tricks
The BIG SHOCK: using 'er' and 'sie' for objects (grammatical gender)

Practice exercises with answers (fill-in, replace, translate, choose)

title: Verb "Sein" in German
description: The German verb "sein" (to be) is the most important verb to build simple sentences.
content: "Sein" (to be) is the most fundamental German verb. It is highly irregular and must be memorized. It is used to describe identity, states, professions, and characteristics. Combined with negation using 'nicht', you can form negative sentences.

examples.english: That is not my book. (nicht before possessive)
I have no money. (kein before noun)

conjugationTable: NICHT → used before verbs, adjectives, definite articles, possessives
errorTraps: Mix 'bin/bist/ist/sind/seid' up and you fail. Memorize them!
Use KEIN for nouns with ein/eine: 'Ich habe kein Auto'
Use NICHT for everything else: 'Ich bin nicht müde'
'nicht' usually goes at the END of a sentence or before the word it negates

title: Verb "Sein" in the Past Tense
description: Learn how to use the verb 'sein' in the past tense (Präteritum) and form questions with it.
content: The past tense (Präteritum) of 'sein' is used very frequently in spoken and written German — unlike most other verbs which prefer Perfekt in spoken German. The past tense forms of 'sein' are: war, warst, war, waren, wart, waren.
subtopics: Forming questions with the verb sein

examples.english: Have you been to Germany before?

conjugationTable: Yes/No: War + Subject + ...? → War er krank?
W-Question: W-Wort + war + Subject + ...? → Wo warst du?
errorTraps: 'war' (was) vs 'waren' (were) — don't confuse singular and plural
For questions, the verb 'war/warst/waren' comes FIRST (yes/no) or SECOND (W-questions)

title: Verb "Haben" in German
description: German counterpart of the English verb "to have": definition, conjugation, examples, questions, and adjective endings.
content: "Haben" (to have) is the second most important German verb. It is used to express possession, and it also serves as a helper verb in the Perfekt tense. Like 'sein', it is irregular and must be memorized. This unit also introduces adjective endings after indefinite articles in the nominative case.
subtopics: A recall of the nominative case
Adjective endings after indefinite articles in the nominative case

examples.english: A tall man. A small cat. (adj. endings after ein/eine)

errorTraps: du haST (not du habst), er/sie/es haT (not habet)
Don't confuse 'haben' with 'sein' — 'Ich habe Hunger' (I have hunger = I am hungry)
Adjective endings after 'ein' are different from after 'der'!

title: German Present Tense
description: Introduction to German regular and irregular verbs, their conjugation rules, and use in sentences.
content: The present tense (Präsens) is the most commonly used tense in German. Regular verbs follow a predictable pattern by removing the -en ending and adding personal endings. Irregular verbs change their stem vowel in the du and er/sie/es forms. Some regular verbs also have small exceptions in their conjugation.
subtopics: Exceptions in the conjugation of regular verbs

The wir and sie/Sie forms NEVER change stem: 'wir fahren' (NOT 'wir fähren')
Verbs ending in -d/-t add extra 'e' before endings: du arbeitest, er arbeitet

title: German Modal Verbs
description: Introduction to German modal verbs, their conjugation in present tense, and use in sentences.
content: Modal verbs express ability, permission, desire, obligation, or necessity. German has six modal verbs: können (can), müssen (must), wollen (want), dürfen (may), sollen (should), and mögen (like). When used with another verb, the modal verb is conjugated and the main verb goes to the END of the sentence in infinitive form.
subtopics: Conjugation of modal verbs in present tense
Questions with modal verbs in German

examples.english: He wants to buy a car.
What do you want to eat?

conjugationTable: können (can): ich kann, du kannst, er kann, wir können, ihr könnt, sie können
müssen (must): ich muss, du musst, er muss, wir müssen, ihr müsst, sie müssen
wollen (want): ich will, du willst, er will, wir wollen, ihr wollt, sie wollen
dürfen (may): ich darf, du darfst, er darf, wir dürfen, ihr dürft, sie dürfen
sollen (should): ich soll, du sollst, er soll, wir sollen, ihr sollt, sie sollen
mögen (like): ich mag, du magst, er mag, wir mögen, ihr mögt, sie mögen
Subject + Modal Verb + ... + Main Verb (infinitive at END)
errorTraps: DO NOT forget the main verb at the END: 'Ich kann Deutsch sprechen' (NOT 'Ich kann sprechen Deutsch')
Modal verbs are irregular — singular forms change stem vowel
In yes/no questions: Modal + Subject + ... + Infinitive? → Kannst du schwimmen?

title: Nominalization of German Verbs
description: Nominalization can be defined as verbs or adjectives acting as nouns. It is a small but important topic in German Grammar.
content: In German, you can turn any verb into a noun by capitalizing it and adding the neuter article 'das'. This process is called nominalization. The resulting noun is always neuter. Nominalized verbs are commonly used in everyday German, especially with phrases like 'beim' (bei + dem) to express ongoing activities.

examples.german: das Schwimmen, das Kochen, das Tanzen

conjugationTable: 1. Take the infinitive: lesen, schreiben, lernen
3. Add 'das': das Lesen, das Schreiben, das Lernen

Don't forget to capitalize: 'das Lernen' (noun) vs 'ich lerne' (verb)

title: Adjective Endings in the Nominative Case
description: Adjective endings in the nominative case after definite articles, indefinite articles, and without articles.
content: In German, adjectives placed before a noun must take an ending that agrees with the noun's gender, number, and the type of article used. The endings differ depending on whether a definite article (der/die/das), an indefinite article (ein/eine), or no article precedes the adjective.

title: German Plural Nouns
description: How to make plural nouns in German? Learn the different plural formation patterns.
content: German plural formation is complex — there is no single rule like adding '-s' in English. Instead, there are several patterns involving different endings and sometimes umlauts. The best approach is to learn the plural form along with each noun, but knowing the patterns helps predict plural forms.

title: Accusative Case in German
description: The most important and widely used case in the German language after nominative.
content: The accusative case marks the direct object — the thing or person directly affected by the verb's action. Only MASCULINE articles change in the accusative (der→den, ein→einen). Feminine, neuter, and plural articles remain the same. Accusative also follows certain prepositions and is used with quantity indicators.
subtopics: Declension of definite articles in accusative case
Declension of indefinite articles in accusative case
Indicators of quantity in German language

examples.english: I drink the milk. (die stays die)
I read the book. (das stays das)
I would like a glass of water. (quantity indicator)

conjugationTable: Feminine: keine → keine | Neuter: kein → kein
errorTraps: Only MASCULINE changes in accusative! der→den, ein→einen
DO NOT change 'die' (feminine) to 'den' — only 'der' (masculine) changes
The question word for accusative is 'wen?' (whom?) for people and 'was?' (what?) for things

title: Accusative Pronouns in German
description: German pronouns decline according to grammatical case. This unit explains pronouns in the accusative case.
content: When pronouns serve as the direct object of a sentence, they take the accusative form. This applies to personal pronouns (mich, dich, ihn...), demonstrative pronouns, possessive pronouns, and reflexive pronouns. Reflexive pronouns are used when the subject and object of a sentence are the same.
subtopics: Personal pronouns in the accusative case
Demonstrative pronouns in the accusative case
Possessive pronouns in the accusative case
Reflexive pronouns in the accusative case

examples.english: He sees me. I see you.

Do you see this man? (demonstrative in accusative)

title: German Accusative Prepositions
description: Prepositions that always take the accusative (indirect object) case.
content: Six German prepositions always require the accusative case. A useful mnemonic to remember them is 'DOGFU B' (durch, ohne, gegen, für, um, bis). Any noun or pronoun following these prepositions must be in the accusative form.

examples.english: I walk through the park. (durch + accusative)
The gift is for you. (für + accusative)
He comes without his brother. (ohne + accusative)
We run around the lake. (um + accusative)
I am against the plan. (gegen + accusative)

conjugationTable: Durch, Ohne, Gegen, Für, Um, Bis
errorTraps: After these prepositions, ALWAYS use accusative: 'für den Mann' (NOT 'für der Mann')
Don't confuse with dative prepositions — these 6 are ALWAYS accusative
'um' for time: 'um 8 Uhr' (at 8 o'clock); 'um' for place: 'um die Ecke' (around the corner)

title: Basic Questions in German
description: Asking questions in German with interrogative pronouns (W-questions).
content: W-questions (W-Fragen) start with a question word (interrogative pronoun) that begins with 'W'. The verb always comes in position 2, immediately after the question word. These questions require a detailed answer and cannot be answered with just 'yes' or 'no'.
subtopics: Wer? / Wen? / Wem? (who? / whom? / to whom? — cases)
Wo? / Woher? / Wohin? (where? — location, origin, destination)
Welcher? / Welche? / Welches? (which? — declining question word)
Womit? / Wofür? / Worüber? (question words with prepositions)
Wie alt / viel / viele / lange (Wie + adjective combinations)

examples.english: To whom are you giving the present?
What do you drive to work with?

errorTraps: Verb ALWAYS in position 2: 'Was machST du?' (NOT 'Was du machst?')
Wo (where) vs Woher (where from) vs Wohin (where to) — three different words!
Wer (who/nominative) vs Wen (whom/accusative) vs Wem (to whom/dative) — case matters!
Welcher changes ending: welcher Mann / welche Frau / welches Kind / welchen Film
Add 'r' after 'wo' when the preposition starts with a vowel: worauf, worüber, woran
Wie viel (uncountable) vs Wie viele (countable) — 'Wie viel Geld' but 'Wie viele Bücher'
NEVER use 'tun' (do) as a helper in questions — 'Was machst du?' NOT 'Was tust du machen?'

title: Yes-No Questions in German
description: Asking questions in German without interrogative pronouns (Yes-No questions).
content: Yes-No questions (Ja/Nein-Fragen) do not use any question word. Instead, the conjugated verb moves to position 1, before the subject. These questions can be answered with 'ja' (yes), 'nein' (no), or 'doch' (yes, contradicting a negative question). The word order is simply inverted from a statement.
subtopics: Questions with modal verbs (können, müssen, dürfen, sollen, wollen, mögen)
The magic word: Doch (contradicting negative questions)
Ja vs Nein vs Doch — complete answer guide

examples.english: Aren't you tired? — Yes I am! (doch contradicts negative)
Are you coming along to the cinema?
Are you getting up early tomorrow?

examples.german: Magst du keinen Kaffee? — Doch, ich mag Kaffee!
examples.english: Don't you like coffee? — Yes, I do like coffee!

conjugationTable: Du sprichst Deutsch. → Sprichst du Deutsch?
Er kommt morgen. → Kommt er morgen?
Sie haben ein Auto. → Haben Sie ein Auto?
Du kannst schwimmen. → Kannst du schwimmen?
Wir müssen arbeiten. → Müssen wir arbeiten?
Du kommst mit. → Kommst du mit?
Sie steht auf. → Steht sie auf?
errorTraps: Verb goes to position 1 (before the subject): 'Sprichst DU' (NOT 'Du sprichst?')
Use 'doch' (not 'ja') to contradict a negative question: 'Hast du kein Geld? — Doch!'
Don't add 'do/does' like English — just invert the verb and subject
Separable prefix stays at the END: 'Kommst du MIT?' (NOT 'Mitkommst du?')
Reflexive pronoun follows the subject: 'Freust du DICH auf...' (NOT 'Freust dich du...')
Always use rising intonation at the end of yes-no questions

title: English-German Similar Words (Cognates)
description: A massive collection of English and German similar words (cognates) to rapidly expand your vocabulary.
content: English and German share a Germanic root. As a result, thousands of words are either identical or very similar. Learning these cognates is the fastest way to build your vocabulary. This lesson provides an extensive list of these similar words.
subtopics: Consonant Shifts (e.g., f -> v, th -> d)
errorTraps: False friends: Gift (poison), nicht (not present!)
False friends: Handy (cell phone), nicht (useful!)
False friends: Chef (boss), nicht (cook!)
